Short-term vs Long-term Strategies

Illustration for short-term vs long-term strategies.

Holding period is one part of a strategy description. Intraday trading generally opens and closes within a session, while swing and longer-term approaches retain exposure across sessions. The labels alone do not define a reliable return, suitable workload or tax outcome.

Compare the time needed to observe and record decisions under each hypothetical approach.
More transactions can increase costs; actual fees and turnover must be measured rather than assumed from a label.
Holding overnight adds exposure to news and gaps. Holding longer does not ensure recovery or eliminate permanent loss.
Tax treatment depends on jurisdiction, product and account; no universal long-term tax advantage is asserted here.
💡
Example

Invented comparison: two approaches each begin at $1,000 and end at $1,020 before costs. If one completes 20 round trips costing $2 each, its ending value is $980; two such round trips leave $1,016. This isolates cost arithmetic and does not establish that either approach could earn the assumed gross result.

Pro Tip

Choose a practice review task, such as comparing planned and observed costs over a fixed period. No number of study hours or selected profitable months certifies readiness for real-money trading.

Return Assumptions and Practice Goals

A practice lesson cannot establish a realistic monthly return from a label such as beginner, intermediate or professional. Outcomes depend on the strategy, exposure, market conditions and costs. A positive practice result is not evidence that the same result can be repeated with real money. Use explicit assumptions for calculations instead of treating a return target as an entitlement.

Separate arithmetic from expectations
State the period: a monthly rate and an annual rate are different inputs.
State whether gains are reinvested and whether deposits or withdrawals occur.
Identify which costs the example includes and which it leaves out.
A comparison with a fund or index needs a defined period, benchmark and method; no fund ranking is established here.
💡
Example

Hypothetical arithmetic: start with $100, gain 10% in month one, then 10% on the new balance in month two. With reinvestment and no costs or cash flows, the balances are $110 and $121. The two-month gain is 21%, not 20%. The assumed gains are inputs, not forecasts.

If a hypothetical 10% gain repeated every month for twelve months, (1.10^12 − 1) × 100 gives about 213.8% annual growth before costs. This shows the compounding implied by the assumption; it does not make such a result typical or achievable.

Losses compound too
💡
Example

A hypothetical $100 balance that falls 10% becomes $90. A subsequent 10% gain brings it to $99, not back to $100. Recovering from $90 to $100 requires a gain of about 11.1%. The order and size of gains and losses matter when reviewing a record.

Use reviewable practice goals
Record the reason for each practice decision before checking its outcome.
Compare the intended position size with the position actually entered.
Review losses as well as gains, and identify missing information.
Track costs and cash flows separately from market gains.
Following a plan makes a decision easier to evaluate; it does not guarantee profit.
Pro Tip

Choose a review task you can verify, such as checking whether each journal entry contains its original reasoning. Avoid requiring yourself to make a fixed number of trades or a fixed profit merely to meet a practice goal. Record uncertainty when the evidence is too limited to draw a conclusion.

Creating a Trading Journal

A journal preserves the reasoning recorded before an outcome. That makes assumptions easier to inspect, but a journal cannot transform an untested idea into a profitable strategy. Record losses and missing information as carefully as gains.

Record symbol, source, time, units, entry price, fees and the original reason.
Distinguish a planned exit from an actual fill and preserve both values.
Separate market gains from deposits, withdrawals and costs.
Note what was known at the decision time; avoid replacing the original reasoning with a story inferred from the outcome.
💡
Example

Invented entry: 50 shares bought at $180 and sold at $185 produce $250 gross, or about 2.78% of the $9,000 purchase notional before costs. A favorable result does not prove that patience, a chart pattern or the written rationale caused it. A comparable losing observation is necessary for an honest review.

Pro Tip

Paper or a local spreadsheet is enough for a journal. TradeHQ Ghost Journal can record a practice rationale; browser storage can be cleared, so keep any important personal record separately. Do not enter private financial credentials.

Evaluating Your Performance

Review a defined observation period, cash flows and costs before comparing results. Total return, realized gains, unrealized changes and trade counts are different measures. A selected winning sample does not establish repeatable skill.

Realized win rate: share of completed outcomes classified as wins under an explicit cost and matching method. Open positions are not completed wins.
Profit factor: sum of realized gains divided by the absolute sum of realized losses. It is not average win divided by average loss; a zero loss denominator has no finite ratio.
Average gain and average loss need units and a matching method. Larger positions can dominate dollar measures.
A Sharpe ratio compares mean excess return with return standard deviation on a compatible frequency. Benchmark, risk-free assumption and annualization affect the number; higher historical values are not a guarantee.
💡
Example

Two gains of $20 and one loss of $10 give profit factor (20 + 20) ÷ 10 = 4. Average gain divided by average loss is 20 ÷ 10 = 2: a different statistic. Costs and the method for closing partial positions can change both.

Pro Tip

TradeHQ displays simulated account observations. Ask which data and method produced a metric; the mentor price-only sale comparison excludes fees and lot matching and is explicitly not a realized win rate.
